title: Relabel the shelves, never the jars
allegory: A tensor is a pantry of jars on numbered shelves; rearrange rewrites the shelf labels and walks the jars into the new layout, but never opens a jar.
map: the new floor plan written on the door
the pattern string 'h w -> w h'
jars never opened, none added or lost
rearrange keeps every element; only the layout changes
merging axes: order inside the brackets matters

chapters.name: The mess
chapters.note: shape (2, 3, 4) ... wait, which one was height?

cap.1: You have a block of numbers and need it in a different layout. Old code does this with bare axis numbers, and it is easy to get wrong.
cap.2: x.transpose(1,2).reshape(2,12) works, but nothing says which axis is which. Change the input shape and it silently does the wrong thing.
cap.3: Positional permute/reshape chains encode layout implicitly. Nothing is checked against intent, so shape-compatible mistakes pass silently.

cap.1: Picture a pantry of jars on labelled shelves. You write the new floor plan on the door, and the jars walk to their new places. No jar is opened.
cap.2: einops makes you name every axis on both sides of an arrow. The library works out the permute and reshape, and checks the names add up.
cap.3: rearrange(x, 'h w -> w h') is a permutation of axes described by name; the pattern is validated against x.shape, so intent is explicit and checked.

cap.1: Left of the arrow: how the shelves are labelled now. Right: how you want them. Brackets tape two labels into one long shelf.
cap.2: 'b h w -> b (h w)' flattens each image into one row. The brackets say: merge h and w, with h as the slow-moving outer index.
cap.3: Parenthesised groups compose axes row-major: (h w) has size h*w with index i*w + j. Unnamed sizes are inferred; ambiguous splits need a keyword, e.g. h=4.

cap.1: Six jars, two shelves of three. Same six jars afterwards, in a new layout. Nothing added, nothing lost, nothing opened.
cap.2: Rearrange only moves elements. The count is always the same before and after, which is exactly what makes it safe to reason about.
cap.3: Element count is invariant (prod of sizes). This is the contrast with einops.reduce (which drops axes) and repeat (which adds them).

chapters.name: The silent bug
chapters.verdict: Same shape, different meaning. Only the names catch it.

cap.1: Taping labels in the wrong order still fits on the shelf. The shapes match, the code runs, and the model quietly learns nothing.
cap.2: In attention you split d_model into heads with 'b s (h d) -> b h s d'. Writing (d h) instead gives the same shape and scrambled heads.
cap.3: Axis-merge order fixes which elements are contiguous. (d h) interleaves heads, so every 'head' mixes all heads' channels; no shape check can catch it.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Flatten images before a linear layer
Read activations by name in interpretability

cap.1: You will do this dozens of times: splitting attention heads, flattening images, reading model insides. Naming the axes is how you stay sure.
cap.2: Every transformer you build splits heads with one rearrange, and interpretability code reads activations with named axes. Clear layout is clear thinking.
cap.3: Named-axis layout is how you keep head, position and batch semantics straight when you start hooking and patching activations to understand and steer models.

coda.title: Tap cells to mark jars, then read how they land after 'h w -> (w h)'

caption.1: Tap a few jars. Then compare where they land when the labels are taped as (h w) versus (w h). Same jars, different order.
caption.2: Mark a row: under (h w) it stays contiguous, under (w h) it spreads out with stride 3. That spread is the head-scrambling bug in miniature.
caption.3: (h w) index = i*W + j; (w h) index = j*H + i. A row is contiguous in the first and strided in the second: the same fact as (h d) vs (d h).

hamming.what: A way to change a tensor's layout by naming its axes instead of numbering them.
hamming.when: Whenever you permute, flatten, split or merge axes, which is most days in ML code.
hamming.why: Names make intent checkable, so shape-compatible mistakes stop being silent.

object.title: The relabelling crate
object.subtitle: A crate of numbered jars you can re-shelve without ever opening one.

cap.1: Twelve jars on three shelves. Each jar's height is its position in the flat line after rearranging.
cap.2: A (3, 4) tensor. Bar height = flat index after 'h w -> (h w)'.
cap.3: Height encodes the flattened index i*W + j under row-major merge.

cap.1: Taped as (h w): heights rise along each shelf. Each shelf is one unbroken run.
cap.2: (h w): rows stay contiguous. Neighbours along w are neighbours in memory.
cap.3: (h w) keeps w as the fast axis: stride 1 along w, stride W along h.

cap.1: Now taped as (w h). Same jars, but the heights rise down the columns instead.
cap.2: (w h): columns are contiguous now. The same shape, a different meaning.
cap.3: (w h) makes h the fast axis: index j*H + i. Shapes agree; semantics do not.

cap.1: This is the attention-head bug: split in the wrong order and each head gets a mix of everyone's numbers.
cap.2: Splitting d_model as (d h) instead of (h d) interleaves heads exactly like this.
cap.3: With (d h), head k receives channels k, k+H, k+2H...: an interleave that no shape assert detects.

predict.q: After 'h w -> (h w)', how many jars change count?

options.t: None: rearrange never adds or drops elements

predict.why: Rearrange only moves elements. Reduce drops them, repeat copies them.

predict.q: (h d) and (d h) give the same shape. Do they give the same heads?

options.t: No, the heads are interleaved differently
Yes, same shape means same data

predict.why: Merge order decides which elements are neighbours. Same shape, different grouping.
